title: Design Log Storage System
statement:
Build a class `LogSystem` that stores log records and lists the ones that fall in a time range at a chosen precision. A timestamp is a string `"Year:Month:Day:Hour:Minute:Second"` whose fields are zero-padded decimal numbers: four digits for the year and two for every other field, for instance `"2017:01:01:23:59:59"`.

- `LogSystem()` creates a system with no logs.
- `put(id, timestamp)` stores one log with that `id` and `timestamp`. No two logs share an `id`.
- `retrieve(start, end, granularity)` returns the `id` of every stored log whose timestamp lies between `start` and `end`, both ends included, when all three timestamps are compared only down to the unit named by `granularity` (`"Year"`, `"Month"`, `"Day"`, `"Hour"`, `"Minute"` or `"Second"`). Units finer than `granularity` are ignored everywhere: with `"Day"`, only the year, month and day of each timestamp matter. If `start` is later than `end` at that precision, no log matches. The ids may be returned in any order.
constraints: At most 500 calls in total are made to put and retrieve

signature.name: LogSystem
methods: List<Integer> retrieve(String start, String end, String granularity)

notes:
## Intuition

Every field of a timestamp has a fixed width and is zero-padded, so comparing two timestamps as plain strings gives the same order as comparing them in time. Granularity then becomes a question of how many characters to look at: `"Year"` keeps the first 4 characters, `"Month"` the first 7 (`"2017:01"`), and so on down to all 19 for `"Second"`. Cutting the start, the end and each log to that prefix turns the query into an ordinary inclusive range check, with no date parsing at all.

## Approach

1. Keep `logs`, a list of `[id, timestamp]` pairs, and `prefixLength`, a map from each granularity to the number of characters it keeps (4, 7, 10, 13, 16, 19).
2. `put(id, timestamp)`: append the pair to `logs`.
3. `retrieve(start, end, granularity)`: look up `length` with `prefixLength.get(granularity)`, then cut `start` and `end` to `low` and `high`.
4. For each stored log, cut its timestamp to `key`; if `low <= key <= high` as strings, add its `id` to `result`.
5. Return `result`.

## Example 1, step by step

After the three `put` calls, `logs` holds ids 1, 2, 3. With `"Year"`, `length = 4`, `low = "2016"` and `high = "2017"`; the keys are `"2017"`, `"2017"` and `"2016"`, all in range, so the ids are 1, 2 and 3. With `"Hour"`, `length = 13`, `low = "2016:01:01:01"` and `high = "2017:01:01:23"`. Keys `"2017:01:01:23"` and `"2017:01:01:22"` fit, but `"2016:01:01:00"` is before `low`, so only ids 1 and 2 come back.

## Complexity

- Time: `put` is O(1); `retrieve` is O(n) for n stored logs (each prefix has at most 19 characters).
- Space: O(n) for the stored logs.

## Pitfalls

- Cut `end` to the granularity too: comparing full timestamps would drop `"2017:01:01:23:30:00"` from an `"Hour"` range ending at `"2017:01:01:23:00:00"`.
- The prefix lengths include the colons (`"Month"` is 7 characters, not 6).
- String comparison is only safe because every field is zero-padded; parsed numbers need their own field-by-field order.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `logs` | every stored `[id, timestamp]` pair |
| `prefixLength` | map from each granularity to how many characters it keeps |
| `length` | characters kept for this query |
| `low`, `high` | `start` and `end` cut to `length` characters |
| `key` | a log's timestamp cut to `length` characters |
| `result` | ids of the logs in range |

narration.3: Every log is kept as an [id, timestamp] pair.

narration.19: Look up the prefix length for the requested granularity in the map.
narration.20: Cut start down to the units that matter...
narration.21: ...and cut end the same way, so the whole of its last unit is included.
narration.24: Cut the log's timestamp to the same precision.
narration.25: Zero-padded strings compare like times, so this is an inclusive range test.

narration.29: Return the ids of all logs in range.
